name: Acitretin
lead: Acitretin is an oral second-generation retinoid, a vitamin A derivative prescribed for severe psoriasis that has not responded to other treatments and, off-label, for several disorders in which skin thickens and scales abnormally, such as ichthyosis, Darier disease and pityriasis rubra pilaris.[1][2] It is the active metabolite of etretinate and is sold under brand names including Soriatane and Neotigason.[1] It is a prescription-only drug in the US, UK, Canada and Australia.[1]

Its link to appearance is through visible skin disease: by slowing the over-production of skin cells and encouraging normal maturation, it can reduce the thick, scaly plaques, hyperkeratosis and pustules that mark these conditions, and trial reports describe improvement in plaque thickness, scaling and redness over weeks to months.[1][2] Patients with lesions on the face, hands, scalp or nails use it as one of the systemic options to smooth and flatten visibly affected skin. It is a treatment for skin disease rather than a cosmetic anti-ageing or acne product, and published studies of purely cosmetic use were not found.

Its best-known risk is severe teratogenicity: the US label carries a boxed warning against use in anyone who is or may become pregnant during treatment or for at least three years afterwards.[14] Common side effects resemble vitamin A excess, including dry skin and lips and hair loss.[1][2]

paras: Acitretin is indicated for severe psoriasis in adults, including pustular and erythrodermic forms, and is generally reserved for refractory cases rather than mild or moderate disease.[1][2] The US label says it should be prescribed only by those knowledgeable in the systemic use of retinoids, and that in women of reproductive potential it should be reserved for non-pregnant patients who are unresponsive to other therapies or for whom other treatments are contraindicated.[14]

Off-label uses described include Darier disease, lamellar ichthyosis, pityriasis rubra pilaris, lichen planus, palmoplantar pustulosis and prevention of non-melanoma skin cancer in high-risk patients such as organ-transplant recipients.[2] Guidelines from the American Academy of Dermatology and the National Psoriasis Foundation, and European guidelines, list acitretin among traditional systemic psoriasis therapies.[3][4][5] A 2024 review of oral psoriasis therapies places acitretin with methotrexate and cyclosporine among the older traditional agents, alongside newer oral options such as apremilast.[15]

For people whose psoriasis, ichthyosis or other keratinisation disorders affect visible skin on the face, scalp, hands and nails, acitretin is one of the systemic options dermatologists use to flatten and smooth scaling skin. A registered trial examined it for nail psoriasis,[9] and others for chronic hand dermatitis and palmoplantar pustulosis.[11][21] Quality-of-life measures in the ichthyosis trial improved over 24 weeks in both treatment arms.[16]
Retinoid-related effects the label and reviews describe, such as dry lips, skin peeling and hair thinning, are also visible, and these are part of how patients and clinicians weigh the drug.[1][14]

Reported common effects include nausea, headache, itching, dry or flaky skin, dry or red eyes, dry or swollen lips, thirst and hair loss.[1] Reviews add raised blood triglycerides, musculoskeletal pain, and, more rarely, liver toxicity, pseudotumor cerebri and pancreatitis, and note that liver function and lipids are monitored during treatment.[2]

The US label describes many reactions as resembling hypervitaminosis A, and reports that of 525 subjects in US trials two had clinical jaundice with raised liver enzymes related to treatment, with normalisation after stopping; two of 1,289 subjects in European trials developed biopsy-confirmed toxic hepatitis.[14] A multicentre study examined effects of acitretin on the liver.[22]

Acitretin is highly teratogenic, with reported malformations of the face, skull, spine, limbs and ears.[1] The US boxed warning says it must not be used by females who are pregnant, intend to become pregnant, or may not use reliable contraception during treatment and for at least three years after stopping, and notes that major fetal abnormalities have been reported with acitretin and etretinate.[14]

Guidance calls for two forms of contraception and avoidance of pregnancy for about three years after stopping, partly because acitretin can be converted back to etretinate in the body, and etretinate persists for a very long time.[1][2] Wikipedia adds that people who have taken it are advised not to donate blood for three years, because the blood could reach a pregnant recipient.[1] Blood-donation deferral lists quoted on a T Nation forum thread give the same three-year wait for acitretin.[24]

Acitretin acts on nuclear retinoic acid and retinoid X receptors, which regulate gene transcription and promote normal keratinocyte differentiation while reducing epidermal overgrowth.[1][2] Oral bioavailability is roughly 60 percent, protein binding exceeds 99.9 percent, and the elimination half-life is about 49 hours.[1] A 1988 trial found that food increases its bioavailability.[18] Clinical improvement is typically described as emerging after two to four weeks or longer, and over weeks to a few months in trials.[1][2]

Etretinate, the earlier drug it replaced, had a half-life of about 120 days and a narrow therapeutic window, which made it difficult to manage; acitretin's much shorter half-life was an advantage, though its conversion back to etretinate keeps the pregnancy-avoidance period long.[1][6]

Roche patented acitretin in Germany in 1974, credited to chemists Werner Bollag, Rudolf Ruegg and Gottlieb Ryser, and it was approved in the United States in 1996.[1] It succeeded etretinate, an earlier retinoid that was withdrawn.[1][6]

Acitretin is prescription-only in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada, a Schedule 4 prescription medicine in Australia, and a Class C2 retinoid in Brazil.[1] Brand names include Soriatane and Neotigason.[1] Strict pregnancy-prevention programmes are tied to its use because of the teratogenicity record.[14]

In lifting and bodybuilding forums such as T Nation, acitretin appears mainly in threads about psoriasis, where members mention Soriatane as a vitamin A derivative used for the condition, often in comparison with isotretinoin, and in lab-result and blood-donation discussions.[23]

A double-blind, placebo-controlled study in renal transplant recipients examined acitretin for skin-cancer prevention and reduction of keratotic lesions, and a multicentre randomized trial examined chemoprevention of non-melanoma skin cancers in renal transplant recipients.[7][19]

A 2024 randomized trial in Chandigarh, India of 64 patients with symptomatic oral lichen planus compared oral acitretin plus topical triamcinolone with triamcinolone plus placebo for 28 weeks with eight further weeks of follow-up, using the Oral Disease Severity Score as the main measure.[20] A 2022 double-blind trial in congenital ichthyosis compared vitamin D with acitretin over 24 weeks in 24 completers; both arms improved on some severity scores and quality of life, with no significant difference between arms and no serious adverse events.[16] A 2025 open-label cohort study compared upadacitinib with acitretin for pustules in palmoplantar pustulosis.[21]

Registered trials have examined acitretin in severe plaque psoriasis (dose-ranging, n=61), nail psoriasis (n=36), combination with etanercept in psoriasis (n=10 and n=60), chronic hand dermatitis (n=9), HIV-associated psoriasis (n=30) and hidradenitis suppurativa versus apremilast (n=70, 2024); several others were withdrawn or terminated.[8][9][10][11][12][13] Reviews report PASI 75 responses of roughly one-third to one-half of patients at 12 weeks in psoriasis trials.[2] No studies were found of acitretin for purely cosmetic purposes.

timeline.event: Acitretin patented in Germany by Roche.[1]
Double-blind placebo-controlled study of acitretin in renal transplant recipients published.[7]
Registered trial of acitretin versus apremilast in hidradenitis suppurativa completed.[13]

card.summary: A prescription oral retinoid for severe psoriasis and keratinisation disorders, with strict pregnancy-prevention rules.
card.note: Highly teratogenic; contraception required during and for about three years after treatment.

quick.overview:
Acitretin is an oral vitamin A-derived drug prescribed for severe psoriasis and certain disorders where skin thickens and scales abnormally.

It is a treatment for skin disease, not an established cosmetic; studies of purely cosmetic use were not found.
quick.mechanism: It binds nuclear retinoid receptors and shifts gene activity so skin cells mature normally and over-multiply less. Its half-life is about two days.
quick.risks: Documented risks include severe birth defects, dry skin and lips, hair loss, raised blood fats and rare liver problems. It is prescription-only, with pregnancy prevention required for about three years after use.

chain: Oral retinoid acts on keratinocyte differentiation
Less thickening, scaling and pustule formation
Smoother, less visibly scaly skin on face, hands, scalp and nails
angle.text: Dermatologists prescribe acitretin when psoriasis or a keratinisation disorder produces thick, scaly or pustular skin that other treatments have not cleared. By normalising how skin cells mature, it can flatten plaques and reduce scale over weeks to months, which changes how affected skin looks.
